Home‑Court Advantage and the Associations of Travel and Jet Lag with Team Performance in the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA)

Josh Leota1,2,3*   , Dean J. Miller4,5,6, Mark É. Czeisler7,8, Jesse Cook9, Luis Mascaro1, Tim D. Smithies4,10, Ayden Nelthropp1 and Elise R. Facer‑Childs1

Abstract Background  Travel-related fatigue and circadian disruption (i.e., jet lag) are well-established factors limiting perfor‑ mance in elite men’s sport and are recognized contributors to home advantage. Yet evidence from women’s profes‑ sional leagues remains scarce. Aim  This study examined temporal trends in home-court advantage and assessed how cumulative travel burden and directional jet lag relate to performance in the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA). Methods  Game location, timing, and performance data from 3489 regular season WNBA games spanning 18 sea‑ sons (2007–2024) were analyzed using mixed-effects models adjusted for game time, team and opponent strength, and season. We quantified cumulative travel distance over the preceding seven days and directional jet lag based on eastward or westward travel adjusted for circadian resynchronization. Results  Home-court advantage declined significantly over time (β =  − 0.67, p = .002), from 64.3% in 2009 to 52.3% in 2024, coinciding with improved league-wide travel conditions. Greater recent travel distance was associated with worse performance among away teams (β = –0.04, p = .020), primarily driven by increased points conceded (β = 0.04, p = .018). Eastward jet lag was significantly associated with worse home team performance (β = –0.15, p = .049), with no such associations observed for westward jet lag or among away teams (all p ≥ .399). Conclusion  These findings provide the first large-scale evidence linking travel and circadian disruption to perfor‑ mance in the WNBA. Although home-court advantage has declined, travel-related challenges persist. Incorporating circadian principles into travel and recovery protocols may help improve performance, particularly as game schedules grow more congested with league expansion.

Key Points

•	 Home-court advantage in the WNBA has progressively declined over the past two decades. •	 Away teams that travelled more in the week leading up to a game performed worse, primarily due to conceding more points to the opposing team.

Introduction Frequent travel across time zones is a defining characteristic of North American professional team sports. Although numerous studies have examined the impact of rapid travel on performance in professional men’s leagues, such as the National Basketball Association (NBA) [1–4], National Football League (NFL) [5, 6], Major League Baseball (MLB) [7–9], and National Hockey League (NHL) [10, 11], research in women’s leagues remains critically understudied, with only limited work examining schedule load [12]. In particular, the impacts of travel direction and distance on team performance have not been systematically studied in the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA). The WNBA was founded in 1996 as an NBA-backed effort to establish a sustainable professional women’s basketball league and featured eight teams in a 28-game regular season in its inaugural season. The league underwent cycles of expansion and contraction of teams and games before landing on a stable 12-team model by the 2010s (and a 13th franchise in 2025) alongside progressive increases in regular season games. The regular season typically runs from mid-May through mid-September involving multiple games per week before playoffs extending into October, aligning with a summer schedule that avoids overlap with the NBA. Absent lucrative media rights deals like the NBA, WNBA franchises operated on relatively smaller operational budgets, combatted in part by a 2022 $75 million capital campaign leading to initiatives including the 2024 league-wide chartered flights program [13]. WNBA athletes face highly demanding schedules that require consistent peak performance and rapid recovery, often under suboptimal travel conditions with repeated logistical disruptions [14]. Indeed, in a 2023 survey of WNBA athletes, most players voted travel as the biggest issue facing the league [15]. Existing research, predominantly conducted in males, indicates cumulative travel fatigue and circadian misalignment (i.e., jet lag) can adversely impact athlete physiology [16] and performance via impaired physical capacity [17, 18] and cognitive function [18]. Travel fatigue and jet lag are common yet distinct consequences of rapid transmeridian travel [19–21]. Travel fatigue is a non-specific cumulative disturbance that can arise after long duration travel, is independent of the

number of time zones crossed, and is characterized by lethargy, changes in mood, and reduced motivation [22, 23]. Travel fatigue arises from the physical and psychological demands of travel, including prolonged uncomfortable seating conditions, psychological stress, reduced oxygen quality, dehydration, and physical inactivity [24, 25]. In contrast, jet lag reflects transient circadian disruption following rapid travel across time zones [26]. Human physiology and behavior are governed by a wide range of endogenously driven circadian rhythms that synchronize to the 24-h environment via the light–dark cycle [27], among other circadian cues. Travel across time zones can desynchronize internal circadian rhythms from the external 24-h environment, causing disruptions to athlete performance and wellbeing [28]. This desynchronosis— or jet lag—persists until internal rhythms entrain to the new 24-h environment, which generally occurs at a rate of 1-h per day [29]. For North American leagues like the WNBA, teams are based at varying longitudes, requiring frequent eastward and westward travel and, therefore, frequent circadian desynchrony. Home-court advantage ([30] for a historical view, see [31]), the tendency for home teams to outperform visiting teams, is a multifactorial phenomenon, with contributing drivers including partisan crowd support, venue familiarity, and travel-related fatigue and circadian misalignment caused by the visiting teams’ travel demands [32–35]. However, existing literature has again primarily focused on male athletes, overlooking potential sexspecific physiological and psychological responses to travel-related stressors. This omission of female-focused research is problematic because females are physiologically distinct and are unlikely to respond identically to travel fatigue or jet lag compared to male athletes, in part due to sex-based differences in sleep and circadian regulation [36–38]. For example, females exhibit an earlier circadian phase angle of entrainment [39] and a shorter intrinsic circadian period [40] relative to males (e.g., 35% of females have average intrinsic circadian periods shorter than 24 h, compared to 14% of males), indicating a circadian system engineered to facilitate phase advances more than delays. In an evolving evidence base, there are also reports of sex differences in light responsiveness and photic resetting [41, 42], which have further implications for entrainment capacity. For travel, these differences suggest that females may, on average, adapt

Beyond the implications of sex differences in biology, there are important structural and cultural sex differences in professional sports leagues. For example, whereas the NBA features fairly consistently timed evening games that reinforce stable, delay-biased circadian entrainment (> 90% games start between 6:00 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. local time [3]), the WNBA schedule exhibits substantially greater day-to-day variability in game timing, including a higher proportion of daytime contests (only 72% of games start between 6:00 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. local time). Increased game-to-game variability in game timing combined with more constrained travel logistics predisposes WNBA teams to more irregular light exposure and behavioral timing, introducing competing phase-shifting signals. Consequently, observed differences in jet lag responses between leagues may relate to schedule- and environment-dependent entrainment dynamics as much as sex differences in physiology. Compounding this issue, WNBA players have historically faced under-resourced and suboptimal travel conditions, including travel via commercial flights, potentially exacerbating fatigue and circadian disruption. Further, collecting data related to circadian rhythmicity in athletes remains logistically and methodologically challenging [38, 43], highlighting the need for innovative research in this area.

Aims of the Study This study presents the first large-scale analysis of homecourt advantage, travel demands, and directional jet lag in the WNBA. Based on 18 years of regular season WNBA games (2007–2024), we aimed to (1) describe temporal trends in home-court advantage; (2) examine the association between recent cumulative travel distance and team performance; and (3) examine the association between directional jet lag and team performance.

Materials and Methods Regular season game data from 18 WNBA seasons (2007–2024) were compiled from ESPN.com using the open-access R package wehoop (v2.1.0) [44]. To verify the accuracy of the publicly available data, we randomly selected 10 games and cross-referenced the date, venue, location, and score against an independent source (the official WNBA website, https://​stats.​wnba.​com). All data from sampled games were consistent. Games from the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) impacted 2020 “Wubble” season were excluded from travel and jet lag analyses due to the absence of travel between

games [45]. Prior seasons were not included due to variations in game structure (the WNBA transitioned from two 20-min halves to four 10-min quarters) and to avoid the compositional disruption caused by the Charlotte Sting dispersal draft prior to the 2007 season. Games representing the WNBA Commissioner’s Cup Final were also excluded due to selection bias toward stronger teams, their playoff-like nature, and their neutral-site locations. Game statistics were missing for four regular season games from the data source and therefore were individually inspected. Two of the four games were missing due to venue changes within the same city; in these cases, box score data were manually retrieved from the official WNBA website (https://​ stats.​wnba.​com/​scores) and added to the dataset. The remaining two games were excluded from analysis due to exceptional circumstances. One was postponed due to poor air quality impacting outdoor conditions in New York City and rescheduled for a later date, with no official box score recorded for the original fixture [46]. The other was a 2018 forfeit, in which the Las Vegas Aces were unable to compete against the Washington Mystics after more than 25 h of commercial travel delays and cancellations, which ultimately resulted in the players unanimously voting not to play and forfeiture of the game [14]. A total of 3489 regular season games (M = 205.24 per season, SD = 14.60) met the inclusion criteria for the travel and jet lag analyses. This study did not require ethical approval from an institutional review board as all data were obtained from publicly available records and human participants were not directly recruited or involved.

Travel Predictors and Game Outcome Variables Travel Distance To quantify travel demands for each WNBA team, we calculated the cumulative travel distance (in miles) over the seven days preceding each regular season game. Game schedules and team box scores were accessed using the wehoop R package (v2.1.0) [44], with location data linked to each team’s home venue. Games were geocoded using U.S.A. city coordinates and team-specific stadium locations. The Haversine formula (i.e., great-circle distance between two points on a sphere) was used to calculate the distance, in miles, between the latitudes and longitudes of each team’s current and previous game locations using the geosphere R package (v1.5.18) [47]. These travel distances were summed within a rolling 7-day window, producing the primary travel distance predictor variable (i.e., total miles traveled over the past seven days).

Directional Jet Lag To estimate potential travel-induced circadian misalignment, directional jet lag was defined as the number of time zones traveled after accounting for a resynchronization rate of 1-h per day (see Fig. 1), as athletes have demonstrated return to baseline performance following sufficient circadian adjustment [3, 8]. Specifically, eastward and westward travel were coded based on the difference in time zone codes between the current and previous game locations. The number of days between games was subtracted from the time zone difference to estimate potential remaining misalignment after resynchronization. If the resulting value was 1 h or more, the game was coded as having eastward or westward jet lag, depending on the direction of travel; otherwise, the game was coded as no jet lag. This approach (used in [3, 4, 8]) follows previous work showing that athletic performance can be impaired by even a 1-h time zone shift [48].

Team Performance Team performance was measured using points differential, calculated as total points scored minus total points conceded. This continuous outcome captures gamelevel variation in performance more sensitively than binary outcomes (e.g., win vs. loss), which may obscure

meaningful differences in team performance. When significant points differential associations were observed, additional models were run to test whether these relationships were primarily driven by team points scored (i.e., changes in offense), team points conceded (i.e., changes in defense), or a combination of both.

Statistical Analysis All analyses were performed in R version 4.3.3 [49]. To examine Aim 1, which explored historical trends in home-court advantage across WNBA regular seasons, we calculated average home win percentage (i.e., the proportion of games won by the home team) and average home points differential (i.e., average game total points scored minus total points conceded) for each season from 2007 to 2024. These values were aggregated at the season level and visualized using line plots to examine temporal changes. To address Aims 2 and 3, we fitted multilevel mixedeffects linear models using the lme4 package (v1.1.36) [50]. The primary outcome was team points differential and the primary predictors were cumulative distance traveled over the past seven days, modeled continuously, and directional jet lag, modeled as a three-level factor (westward vs. eastward vs. no jet lag). Results Trends in WNBA Home Advantage The WNBA regular season home winning percentage (β = −0.67, 95% CI [−1.06, −0.28], t =  − 3.60, p = 0.002, R2 = 0.45) and average home points differential (β = −0.63, 95% CI [–1.04, –0.22], t =  − 3.23, p = 0.005, R2 = 0.40) declined significantly over the 18-season observation

period (Table 2 and Fig. 2A–B). From 2007 through 2017, home teams won ≥ 55% of games in 10 of 11 (91%) seasons, peaking in 2009 at 64.3%. In contrast, from 2018 through 2024, home teams won ≥ 55% of games in just one of seven (14%) seasons, reaching a low of 51.7% in 2023. Notably, home winning percentage was exactly 50.0% in the pandemic-impacted 2020 season which saw all games played at a neutral venue. Home points differential followed a similar downward trend, peaking in 2009 at a + 4.0 points per game advantage and declined to just + 0.8 points per game advantage by 2024. There also appeared to be a subtle biennial fluctuation in home advantage, with lower home win percentages observed in even-numbered years.

Specifically, greater travel distance in the week preceding a game was significantly associated with worse points differential for away but not home teams. This finding was seemingly driven by opponents scoring more points as cumulative travel distance increased, which may reflect degraded defensive performance, or other in-game performance consequences of travelrelated impairment. Further, we observed significantly worse home (but not away) team performance when experiencing eastward (but not westward) jet lag. These findings in the WNBA build upon the existing literature related to travel and professional sport performance, which has predominantly been performed in the context of male professional sports [54]. Importantly, the associations observed are generally consistent with previous work performed in male athletes.

Trends in WNBA Home Advantage Home-court advantage in the WNBA declined steadily from 2009 to 2024, consistent with attenuation of homecourt advantages over time observed in other professional sports leagues [55, 56]. One potential explanation is that improvements in travel conditions and the broader professionalization of sports leagues have reduced the physical and psychological burdens traditionally associated with playing on the road [54, 57]. Travel conditions in the WNBA have changed significantly since the league’s first season in 1997. For example, under the WNBA’s 2020 collective bargaining agreement, players were guaranteed upgraded travel provisions, including comfort or economy plus seats on airlines and individual hotel rooms when travelling [58]. More recently, beginning with the 2024 season, the WNBA implemented full-time charter flights for all teams, driven in part by concerns over player health and safety [13]. Consistent with these improved travel conditions, home-court advantage from 2021 to 2024 averaged 53.0%, only onethird of what it was from the 2007 to 2019. These travel and accommodation advancements may have partly contributed to the reduced home-court advantage across the most recent seasons observed in the current study. Home winning percentage and home points differential exhibited biannual fluctuations, with higher-magnitude differences in odd calendar years particularly between 2009 and 2019. Systematic differences intrinsic to the WNBA league scheduling are unlikely to account for these fluctuations, as teams hosted and visited an approximately equal number of games per season and team performance varied over time. One explanation  could be Olympic and FIBA World Championship tournament years, which occur selectively on even calendar years. Star WNBA player participation in these tournaments

may result in more league parity due to scheduling impacts (a month-long hiatus on Olympic years and earlier season in FIBA World Championship years) and star player absences (from practices and team events, if not games). The fluctuations appear diminished during 2021 to 2024, suggesting that the same or co-occurring factors associated with the decline in home-court advantage have also influenced these fluctuations. Moreover, fluctuations may be reduced as a result of smaller-magnitude home-court advantages. The pandemic-disrupted 2020 WNBA season, which took place in a single-site “Wubble” environment in Bradenton, Florida, altered multiple aspects of home versus away team dynamics. Living in the Bubble and effectively eliminating travel minimized potential jet lag effects, and no home-court advantage was observed. Similar patterns were observed in the NBA during the same period, where the removal of travel was linked to the elimination of home-court advantage [59, 60]. However, the removal of in-person fans during these seasons also removed the potential influence of home crowd support, making it difficult to disentangle the specific effects of travel from crowd support on home-court advantage [33]. In-person fans returned in the 2021 WNBA season (except for Indiana Fever home games), but travel was reduced amid the pandemic by implementing twogame mini-series [61]. During that season, home-court advantage remained relatively low (53.9%), suggesting a reduced travel burden may have continued to dampen the typical benefits associated with playing at home.

Travel Distance and WNBA Team Performance Greater accumulated travel distance across the week preceding a game was associated with worse points differential for away (but not home) teams. This finding suggests that cumulative travel is associated with adverse effects on team performance, consistent with prior studies linking travel fatigue to reduced athletic performance [62, 63]. The association was driven by an increase in points conceded by away teams, suggesting travel fatigue may disproportionately impair defensive, rather than offensive, performance. However, alternative in-game factors could have been affected, contributing to more points conceded. For example, a team may make more offensive turnovers or commit more fouls. As such, this association may not only reflect degraded defensive performance, but rather overall game performance that translates into more points conceded. This defense-specific relationship is consistent with the cognitive and psychological demands of defensive play. Successful defensive execution relies on rapid and reactive decision-making in response to dynamic offensive actions, potentially making it more sensitive

In contrast, offensive sets are often more structured and rehearsed and, at times, directed by the sideline coaching staff, potentially buffering them from the same performance declines. Away teams in our study often faced suboptimal travel conditions relative to male professional sports leagues. In August 2018, the Las Vegas Aces forfeited their game against the Washington Mystics after enduring over 25 h of travel delays and cancelled commercial flights. The decision to forfeit was made on the grounds of player safety, with players and coaches citing excessive travel fatigue and increased injury risk [14]. Earlier collective bargaining agreements prohibited chartered flights as it was deemed an unfair competitive advantage. In 2022, the New York Liberty were fined $500,000, the most in league history, and risked termination for chartering flights for their players in the 2021 season [65]. In 2024, in response to ongoing concerns about player safety, and amid the league’s growing popularity, the WNBA announced a $25 million per year investment to fund full-time charter flights for all teams [13].

Directional Jet Lag and WNBA Team Performance Home teams had a significantly worse points differential when playing with eastward jet lag compared to no jet lag. The magnitude of this difference (−1.86 points per game) is twice as large as the difference between the 6th (−2.68, Indiana Fever) and 9th (−3.30, Phoenix Mercury) best points differentials during the 2024 WNBA regular season. There was no association when playing with westward jet lag, nor when playing on the road. These findings are consistent with previous research that demonstrated eastward- and home-specific associations with impaired performance in the NBA [3] and MLB [8]. Human circadian rhythms can be shifted earlier through a phase advance or later through a phase delay [66]. As the average human endogenous circadian period is slightly longer than 24 h, humans have a natural tendency to delay rather than advance [67, 68]. As a result, westward travel, which typically requires a phase delay, is generally easier to adapt to than eastward travel, which typically requires a more difficult phase advance [69]. The performance decline observed in the current study may reflect biological challenges associated with phase advancing the circadian clock following rapid eastward travel [23, 70]. Such phase advances require athletes to fall asleep and wake up earlier than their homeostatic and circadian drives for sleep would otherwise signal, resulting in a mismatch between internal physiological rhythms and external cues (e.g., light). This circadian misalignment can disrupt sleep, reduce alertness, and

negatively impact performance and motivation, particularly within 72 h of arriving in the new time zone [17]. Eastward travel disadvantage is not unique to basketball, with similar effects being observed in college football [71], international soccer [72], and elite female skeleton athletes [73]. Despite shorter intrinsic circadian periods and photic response profiles that would theoretically favor more efficient phase advances in females, eastward travel and home-game contexts are consistently associated with impaired performance across both the WNBA and NBA. These findings suggest that shared structural and environment-driven factors such as travel logistics, schedule congestion and variability, and behavioral constraints may outweigh potential sex-based differences in circadian physiology. We did not observe an association between eastward or westward travel and performance among away teams, consistent with previous work [3, 8]. One explanation may be that away teams benefit from more structured environments during travel as compared to at home. Team management can proactively manage sleep–wake schedules, training loads, meal timings, and recovery protocols, which may help alleviate potential jet lag symptoms [21, 23, 74]. Away teams may purposefully maintain alignment with their home time zone during short trips—scheduling meals, light exposure, physical activity, and sleep accordingly—to minimize circadian disruption (i.e., “time zone maintenance”). In contrast, players returning to their home time zones may experience greater disruptions to their routines as they depart for their individual homes and attend to family and social obligations.

Practical Applications These findings have practical applications for athletes and support staff. Away teams that accumulate greater travel distance in the week preceding a game showed worse defensive performance. Practitioners could consider circadian-informed scheduling of training loads, light exposure, and sleep timing to facilitate adaptation prior to competition [21]. Similar considerations should be made for home teams travelling eastward in the days preceding a home game. At the league level, these findings emphasize the value of schedule design that minimizes consecutive cross-time zone travel, particularly for away fixtures, and supports the continued implementation of travel provisions such as charter flights introduced under the 2024 collective bargaining agreement. Importantly, these recommendations should be interpreted in the context of the broader home-court advantage landscape; travel and jet lag are likely contributors to, rather than sole determinants of,

Study Strengths This research draws on nearly two decades of WNBA regular season game data (2007–2024) to present the most comprehensive longitudinal analysis of travel, jet lag, and team performance in the women’s professional basketball to date. Second, unlike the vast majority of sports and exercise science research which centers on men athletes, this study addressed an important gap by focusing on professional women athletes, a critically underrepresented population in the field [75]. Third, by using multilevel mixed-effects models with teams and opponents nested within seasons and covariate adjustment for game time, team relative win rate, recent schedule congestion, and prior game performance, our analysis accounted for structural changes in the league over time and adjusted for variation in contextual factors such as competition timing and team strength.

Study Limitations and Future Directions Consistent with established approaches in chronobiology and sports science and in an effort to improve reproducibility and comparisons with published literature, we estimated travel fatigue and circadian misalignment via directional jet lag at the team level via generalizations about travel time and individual circadian biology. This approach, featuring a uniform 1-h per day resynchronization rate, does not account for inter- and intraindividual heterogeneity in circadian phase, circadian sensitivity, and sleep–wake behavior, which have been shown to moderate performance responses to travel [76, 77]. Our team-level estimates should thus be interpreted as approximations of average circadian misalignment rather than exact individual-level risk. Future research should incorporate player-level data (e.g., continuous sleep–wake monitoring, menstrual cycle and circadian phase assessments) to better quantify this association. Additionally, future research should explore whether travel fatigue and circadian disruption affect professional WNBA players’ health and wellbeing beyond on-court performance. Emerging evidence suggests that female athletes may be particularly vulnerable to poor physical and mental health outcomes when exposed to disrupted sleep, irregular sleep patterns, and circadian misalignment [38, 78]. Given the WNBA’s condensed travel schedules and comparatively limited support resources, players may disproportionately face psychological

challenges relative to athletes in better-funded professional sports leagues. This study focused on relationships between travel predictors and global indicators of game performance (e.g., total point differential, points scored, and points conceded), which reflect only a subset of basketball performance outcomes. Future research examining relationships between travel-related dynamics and more granular features of basketball performance, such as free throw percentage, turnovers, steals, personal fouls, and rebounding rate, may provide unique insight into the impact of travel on specific components of basketball performance. Indeed, examples of such granularity exist in studies examining the association between travel and performance in male basketball competitions [1–3, 60, 79]. Travel distance and jet lag estimates were calculated based on game locations only, as team travel itineraries are not publicly available due to privacy considerations. Therefore, our travel and jet lag estimates are underpinned by the conservative assumption that teams departed for their next game destination immediately following each game. To the extent that teams departed later, arrived closer to tip-off, and therefore spent less time in the destination time zone before the game, our estimates of travel demands and circadian resynchronization time may underestimate the true impact of travel and circadian disruption. Team training venues and practice schedules are also not publicly available, and it is possible that some travel occurred between training and competition venues that is not captured in our estimates. Future research working directly with teams could integrate travel itineraries and training data to refine these estimates. Although our models adjusted for opponent and team strength, recent schedule congestion, and travel demands as independent covariates, residual contextual confounding may remain, and findings reported here should be interpreted as adjusted average associations. Finally, although we adjusted for serial dependence by including each team’s prior-game points differential, we did not model a formal residual autocorrelation structure. Future research could extend these findings via alternative modeling frameworks, such as logistic mixed-effects models with binary win/loss outcomes, explicit autocorrelation structures, or lagged-effect specifications.

Conclusion The present study is the first to examine over 3,400 regular season WNBA games from 2007–2024 to describe long-term trends in home-court advantage and examine associations between travel and jet lag on team performance. Home-court advantage has declined, although travel-related factors remain associated with team

Greater travel distance in the week preceding a game was associated with poorer away team performance, while eastward jet lag was associated with poorer home team performance, revealing that teams face distinct travel-related challenges when playing at home and as visitors. As the WNBA expands and with expectations for an increasingly demanding schedule [80], there remains an important need for more research in this population and league initiatives that incorporate sleep and circadian biology into scheduling as well as teamwide and athlete-specific strategies to mitigate travel fatigue and jet lag.

Main Text 54 55 Introduction 56 57 Conceptualization of sleep health has evolved from a focus on the absence of diagnosable 58 disorders to a multidimensional construct, with core components of duration, satisfaction, daytime 59 alertness, efficiency, timing, and regularity (3–7). Sleep regularity has garnered increased 60 attention as measures of intraindividual variability in dimensions of sleep health, rather than mean 61 measures alone, have demonstrated distinct health implications, a point reinforced by a 2024 62 National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel, which concluded that sleep 63 regularity is important for health, safety, and performance (8, 9). 64 65 Traditional metrics of sleep regularity (e.g., standard deviations of bedtime, wake time, or 66 duration) are constrained by their reliance on multi-day averages or conventional dispersion 67 measures and by the implicit assumption of a single main sleep episode (10). These limitations 68 are particularly pronounced when characterizing sleep regularity among individuals with multiple 69 daily sleep episodes (e.g., primary nocturnal sleep plus daytime naps), irregular work hours (e.g., 70 shift work), abrupt phase shifts (e.g., social or travel-associated jet lag (11)) unconventional 71 cycles (e.g., polyphasic sleep (8)), which contribute to circadian disruption that is not necessarily 72 reflected in measures such as the standard deviation of nocturnal sleep duration. Incidentally, 73 these scenarios are prevalent due to modern social and occupational demands (12), shift work 74 (13), and widespread evening use of light�emitting devices (14), all of which can contribute to 75 irregular daily schedules with misalignment between internal biological time and external 76 demands. 77 78 These limitations were addressed with the development of the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) (10, 79 15), which quantifies the probability of being in the same state (asleep or awake) at the same 80 clock time on consecutive days, capturing day-to-day sleep regularity accommodating multiple 81 sleep bouts and sudden schedule changes across the 24�hour cycle. High day-to-day variability 82 in sleep-wake timing as measured by the SRI is prospectively associated with higher rates of all- 83 cause mortality and cause-specific mortality due to cardiometabolic disease and cancer (1, 16, 84 17). These relationships, which appear robust to adjustment for sleep duration and are observed 85 across multiple antecedent risk states (9, 18–23), are hypothesized to reflect a combination of 86 harmful effects of recurrent inconsistencies in the patterns of environmental exposures (e.g., light- 87 dark cycles (15, 24, 25)), behaviors (e.g., sleep-wake, feeding-fasting cycles), and circadian 88 rhythms (i.e., endogenous time-varying physiology (10, 15)). Discussion 275 276 In this study of 506,582 person-days of accelerometer-derived sleep-wake data collected from 277 73,647 middle-aged adults (female n = 41,489 [56.3%]), despite numerically similar median 278 scores, females exhibited a more favorable distribution of day�to�day sleep-wake timing than did 279 males, with greater representation in the highest SRI group and lower representation in the 280 lowest group. Over a median 7.5-year follow-up interval, consistent with recent literature (1, 16), 281 less regular day�to�day sleep-wake timing was associated with higher all-cause and cause- 282 specific mortality rates; however, we report for the first time that these associations differed both 283 between and within sexes. Between�sex comparisons revealed that among the least regular 284 sleepers, all-cause mortality risk was approximately twice as high in males as in females, 285 whereas risk did not differ between sexes among the most regular sleepers. Within�sex 286 comparisons showed stronger SRI-mortality associations in males than females, with significance 287 persisting after adjustment for demographics, baseline health, and health behaviors (i.e., 288 smoking, alcohol, physical activity, sleep duration) among males (e.g., all-cause mortality aHR = 289 1.8 [1.2–2.5]; p <0.001) but not females. These sex-specific dose-dependent SRI-mortality 290 associations suggest that males may have excess vulnerability to highly irregular sleep�wake 291 cycles and their environmental and circadian correlates beyond mechanisms shared by both 292 sexes. 293 294 Our findings reveal that on average, males both exhibit more extreme irregularity in day�to�day 295 sleep-wake timing and experience heightened mortality risks at high levels of irregularity, 296 resulting in the steeper observed SRI-mortality relationships. The potential mechanisms 297 underlying these hypothesis-generating findings warrant investigation. Sex differences in 298 environmental, occupational, and social exposures; clustering of health behaviors, circadian 299 biology, and sleep physiology; and cardiometabolic and inflammatory responses may together 300 shape exposure to and consequences of highly irregular sleep-wake patterns. For example, 301 highly irregular versus regular day-to-day sleep-wake timing is associated with later dim-light 302 melatonin onset and lower amplitude light-dark exposure rhythms (15, 25). With light-dark cycles 303 serving as the principal circadian synchronizer in mammals (51, 52), circadian dysregulation has 304 been proposed to account for why suboptimal light exposure profiles (53) have been associated 305 with higher prospective rates of mood disorders (54), cardiometabolic disease (55–58), and 306 mortality (24). 307 308 Between�sex comparisons showed that the higher male mortality risk was attenuated by high 309 sleep regularity. Males in the least regular SRI group exhibited twice the all-cause mortality rate 310 of similarly irregular females, whereas mortality rates were not significantly different by sex in the 311 most regular SRI group, suggesting that higher sleep regularity may protect against excess male 312 mortality risk. Attenuation of excess male mortality among the most regular sleepers was 313 particularly evident for cardiovascular mortality. Through early September 2025, ischemic heart 314 disease was the leading cause of male death in the UK Biobank, with more than twice as many 315 deaths as those attributable to the second�leading cause (59). In contrast, ischemic heart 316 disease ranked fourth among females, trailing two cancers (lung, breast) and dementia. Irregular 317 sleep confers greater cardiometabolic risk through chronic circadian misalignment (26, 60), 318 autonomic nervous system imbalances with sympathetic overactivation (26), impaired nocturnal 319 blood pressure dipping (61, 62), and adverse metabolic and inflammatory profiles (38, 63), all of 320 which contribute to atherosclerosis, arrhythmogenesis, and ultimately ischemic heart disease 321 (64). 322 323 Given higher baseline cardiometabolic morbidity and less favorable autonomic and vascular 324 aging trajectories among males than among females (65), more regular sleep-wake timing may 325 stabilize these pathways in males, disproportionately reducing their risk of ischemic heart disease 326 and narrowing the male-female cardiovascular mortality disparity that is otherwise observed in the 327 UK Biobank. Our identification of a sex difference in the relationship between the day-to-day regularity of 385 sleep-wake timing and mortality extends a rapidly expanding literature (50), which has thus far 386 largely examined associations between SRI and health or performance at the population or 387 sample level rather than characterizing how these relationships differ within population 388 subgroups. Three recent studies (one peer-reviewed) have reported sex differences in 389 associations between low SRI and health outcomes (2, 45, 48). The peer-reviewed study, 390 published in 2026, found that among 7,085 US adults in the National Health and Nutrition 391 Examination Survey, the highest versus lowest SRI quintile was associated with 8% lower BMI, 392 with a stronger relationship among females (48). In a 2025 conference abstract, among UK 393 Biobank participants (n = 69,725), lower SRI scores were reported to be associated with a higher 394 rate of new-onset heart rhythm disorders (e.g., cardiac arrhythmias and conduction disorders), a 395 relationship that was most pronounced among male participants and especially those with 396 baseline cardiovascular disease (45). A 2026 preprint reported a PheWAS with the SRI among 397 UK Biobank participants (n = 60,998), identifying that 131 of 199 (65.8%) conditions were 398 predicted by SRI (2). Both studies found sex-specific risk elevation of similar magnitude for 399 cardiac dysrhythmias among males as compared to females (2, 45). 400 401 Interestingly, the PheWAS study of new�onset conditions diagnosed one or more years after 402 accelerometer recording found that circulatory disorders were among those most consistently 403 linked with irregular sleep among females but not males (2). A similar sex difference was found 404 for a related circadian exposure; brighter night-time light exposure was more strongly associated 405 with incident coronary artery disease and heart failure in females compared to males (55, 57). 406 These patterns may reflect slower vascular aging (65) allowing sleep� and circadian-associated 407 subclinical cardiometabolic disease to accumulate and manifest as incident diagnoses later in life, 408 especially as potential protective effects of estrogen dissipate with peri-menopause and 409 menopause (74). In independent cohorts, early estrogen depletion through hysterectomy and 410 bilateral oophorectomy has been associated with increased all-cause and cardiovascular 411 mortality in women who had never used estrogen therapy but not in past and current users (75, 412 76). Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58271-x Dose-response relationship between evening exercise and sleep

Josh Leota 1 , David M. Presby2,3,4, Flora Le1, Mark É. Czeisler 5, Luis Mascaro 1, Emily R. Capodilupo2, Joshua F. Wiley1, Sean P. A. Drummond 1, Shantha M. W. Rajaratnam1 & Elise R. Facer-Childs 1

Public health guidelines recommend exercise as a key lifestyle intervention for promoting and maintaining healthy sleep function and reducing disease risk. However, strenuous evening exercise may disrupt sleep due to heightened sympathetic arousal. This study examines the association between strenuous evening exercise and objective sleep, using data from 14,689 physically active individuals who wore a biometric device during a one-year study interval (4,084,354 person-nights). Here we show later exercise timing and higher exercise strain are associated with delayed sleep onset, shorter sleep duration, lower sleep quality, higher nocturnal resting heart rate, and lower nocturnal heart rate variability. Regardless of strain, exercise bouts ending ≥4 hours before sleep onset are not associated with changes in sleep. Our results suggest evening exercise—particularly involving high exercise strain—may disrupt subsequent sleep and nocturnal autonomic function. Individuals aiming to improve sleep health may beneﬁt from concluding exercise at least 4 hours before sleep onset or electing lighter strain exercises within this window.

The relationship between exercise and sleep is symbiotic and complex. Theoretical models of healthy sleep function point to a number of physiological and psychological processes implicated in the sleeppromoting beneﬁts of exercise, including the regulation of core body temperature1, mood2, metabolic expenditure3, and the circadian system4. However, acute strenuous exercise performed close to bedtime may induce prolonged sympathetic activation, e.g., increased heart and respiration rate, and therefore disrupt sleep5,6. As a result, traditional and contemporary sleep guidelines have discouraged strenuous exercise in the hours before bedtime7–9. Recent meta-analytical evidence contradicts the view that evening exercise disrupts sleep. Engaging in evening exercise generally10 and high-intensity evening exercise speciﬁcally11 was not associated with decreases in sleep duration or quality. Although studies have examined the effects of evening exercise intensity or duration in isolation12, no studies to our knowledge have examined the combination of

exercise intensity and duration (i.e., exercise strain). High intensity, long duration (i.e., strenuous) evening exercise is metabolically demanding and may result in an inadequate recovery window before bedtime, limiting the brain and body’s ability to return to the psychophysiological conditions compatible with sleep13. Indeed, researchers who have systematically reviewed the evening exercise literature have recommended future studies focus on the intensity by duration interaction2,14, particularly given most past studies included only lower levels of exercise strain10. High exercise strain (i.e., cardiometabolic demand) is characterized by increased sympathetic activity15, e.g., increased excess post-exercise oxygen consumption16, core body temperature17, heart rate18, and cognitive arousal19. Following exercise, the autonomic nervous system (ANS) facilitates sympathetic withdrawal and parasympathetic re-activation20. Results Demographics The study population included 14,689 participants logging an average of 122.98 exercises (SD = 53.74) across the 1-year study. Baseline characteristics (Table S1) included age (M = 37.89, SD = 10.81), gender (10,845 [73.83%] men), weight (M = 80.39 kilograms, SD = 15.10), and height (1.76 meters, SD = 0.94).

Exercise timing relative to habitual sleep onset Tables S2–6 present estimated marginal means (EMMs) and Tables S7- 11 present strain vs. no-exercise contrasts for all analyses.

Sleep onset When exercise concluded ≥6-h before social jet lag- and seasonalityadjusted habitual sleep onset (i.e., the average sleep onset corresponding to weekdays or weekends, as appropriate, across the calendar month), maximal exercise was associated with earlier sleep onset compared to lower levels of strain and non-exercise days. When exercise concluded 4- to 6-h before habitual sleep onset, sleep onset following light or moderate exercise was similar to non-exercise days. When exercise concluded 4-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, sleep onset became progressively later for all levels of strain and was more pronounced when strain was higher. Engaging in maximal exercise instead of light exercise is associated with a 36.0-minute later sleep onset if the exercise ended 2-h before habitual sleep onset, and an 80.0-minute later sleep onset if the exerciseended 2-h after habitual sleep onset (Fig. 1A; Table 1).

Sleep duration When exercise concluded ≥6-h before habitual sleep onset, exercise strain was positively correlated with sleep duration. In contrast, when exercise concluded 6-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, sleep duration progressively reduced for all levels of strain and was more pronounced when strain was higher. Engaging in maximal exercise instead of light exercise is associated with a 5.4% (22.2 minute) shorter sleep duration if the exercise ended 2-h before habitual sleep onset, and a 13.9% (42.6 minute) shorter sleep duration if the exercise ended 2-h after habitual sleep onset (Fig. 1B; Table 2).

Sleep quality When exercise concluded ≤8-h before habitual sleep onset, increased strain was associated with decreased sleep quality. When exercise concluded 2-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, sleep quality became progressively worse for all levels of strain and was more pronounced when strain was higher. Engaging in maximal exercise instead of light exercise is associated with a 0.87 percentage point decrease in sleep quality if the exercise ended 2-h before habitual sleep onset, and a 5.6 percentage point decrease in sleep quality if the exercise ended 2-h after habitual sleep onset (Fig. 1C; Table 3).

Nocturnal RHR Regardless of when exercise concluded, higher strain was associated with higher RHR. All levels of exercise strain were associated with higher RHR compared to non-exercise days. When exercise concluded 4-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, RHR became progressively higher for all levels of strain and was more pronounced when strain was higher. Engaging in maximal exercise instead of light exercise is associated with a 6.8% (3.9 beats/min) increase in RHR if the exercise ended 2-h before habitual sleep onset, and a 15.0% (9.4 beats/min) increase in RHR if the exercise ended 2-h after habitual sleep onset (Fig. 1D; Table 4).

Nocturnal HRV Regardless of when exercise concluded, higher strain was associated with lower HRV. All levels of exercise strain were associated with lower HRV compared to non-exercise days. When moderate, high, and maximal exercise concluded 4-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, HRV became progressively lower and was more pronounced when strain was higher. When light exercise concluded 2-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset, HRV became progressively lower. Engaging in maximal exercise instead of light exercise is associated with a 14.1% (8.3 unit) decrease in HRV if the exercise ended 2-h before habitual sleep onset, and an 32.6% (14.6 unit) decrease in HRV if the exercise ended 2-h after habitual sleep onset (Fig. 1E; Table 5).

Exercise timing relative to actual sleep onset Secondary analyses examining exercise timing to actual sleep onset were consistent with the primary analyses above. Speciﬁcally, the combination of higher exercise strain and later exercise timing relative to actual sleep onset that night was dose-dependently associated with shorter sleep duration, lower sleep quality, higher nocturnal RHR, and lower nocturnal HRV (Fig. 2A-D).

Exploratory analyses: gender, age, and BMI status The associations of interest between exercise timing and strain, and sleep and nocturnal autonomic activity did not differ across gender (Figs. S1 and S2), age (Figs. S3 and S4), or BMI status (Figs. S5 and S6).

Discussion This large-cohort, multi-national study examined whether exercise strain and exercise timing would demonstrate dose-response relationships with objective sleep and nocturnal autonomic activity in freeliving conditions. Results showed the combination of higher exercise strain and later exercise timing was dose-dependently associated with delayed sleep onset, shorter sleep duration, lower sleep quality, higher RHR, and lower HRV. Evening exercise—particularly involving high levels of cardiovascular strain—may disrupt subsequent sleep and nocturnal autonomic function, thereby impairing a critical stage of the recovery process25. Our ﬁndings are consistent with research on physiological recovery after exercise. The dynamic recovery duration (i.e., timecourse of parasympathetic re-activation) is proportionate to the level of homeostatic stress of the exercise session15. We found higher levels of exercise strain were associated with increased nocturnal RHR and decreased nocturnal HRV several hours after exercise cessation. The initiation and maintenance of healthy sleep function is characterized by parasympathetic activity (e.g., declines in RHR and core body temperature, increases in HRV)22,26. Therefore, when parasympathetic re-activation is disrupted due to increased exercise strain or later exercise timing, sleep may be both delayed in timing and impaired in quality. To minimise disruptions to sleep, individuals should allow for adequate recovery time proportionate to the level of strain achieved in an evening exercise session. When exercise concluded 6–10 hours before habitual sleep onset, nocturnal HRV was slightly lower compared to non-exercise days.

This ﬁnding has important implications for elite and professional athletes, as many competitions that require high and maximal levels of strain are scheduled in the evening due to broadcasting rights. These evening competitions may be jeopardizing athlete sleep and recovery on nights it is needed most. The present study had limitations that should be considered. The biometric device did not detect when sleep was ﬁrst attempted; therefore, we were unable to estimate the time participants began to attempt sleep or calculate sleep onset latency. Future research could collect self-reported timing of attempted sleep or use behavioural devices that record conscious responses to stimuli to investigate whether heightened sympathetic arousal associated with strenuous evening exercise increases sleep onset latency. The summated-heartrate-zones score (SHRZS) method for quantifying exercise strain may underestimate the relative metabolic strain of strength training that involves very brief durations of high-effort movements. Future research could examine the effects of different types of evening strength training (e.g., Olympic lifting). We were unable to control for potential confounds known to impact sleep, such as bright light exposure. Although we can take some conﬁdence in our results given we observed a consistent dose-response relationship in the evening and bright light exposure likely does not covary with exercise strain, future research could measure and control for light exposure. Finally, election of only physically active adults created a sample that is not representative across the spectrum of physical activity levels. Future research could explore the extent to which our ﬁndings apply to the lower end of the physical activity spectrum. We predict the relationship between strenuous evening exercise and sleep to be even stronger in this group, as post-exercise autonomic recovery typically occurs less rapidly in individuals who train less frequently21, have lower levels of cardiovascular ﬁtness27, and have lower resting vagal control35. This study had several strengths. Previous studies on evening exercise and sleep have relied on small sample sizes (M = 12 participants/ study)10 for brief periods, often in laboratory settings. This study examined data from a large sample (14,689 physically active participants) across one year (4,084,354 person-nights) in a real-world setting. These free-living conditions allowed participants to engage in exercises that varied widely in exercise strain. The analyses controlled for important individual differences in sleep and exercise strain. For example, instead of using clock time, exercise timing was calculated relative to each individual’s habitual sleep onset on a given day (thus considering individual, seasonal, and weekday changes in sleep timing) as well as each individual’s actual sleep onset on that night (Fig. 2). Similarly, exercise strain was quantiﬁed from real (as opposed to planned) exercise relative to each individual’s cardiovascular ﬁtness level. This large cohort study of ~4-million-person-nights demonstrates that exercise strain and exercise timing have dose-response relationships with sleep and autonomic activity. To optimize sleep, individuals should aim to complete bouts of exercise four or more hours before their sleep onset to minimise potential adverse consequences to their sleep. If exercising within a 4-h window of sleep onset, individuals could elect to engage in light strain exercises to mitigate sleep and ANS disruption. This study has signiﬁcant implications for public health messaging around timing, duration, and intensity of exercise and presents a critical step towards improving population sleep health.

Methods This large retrospective cohort study adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE)

guidelines and was approved by Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee (#32928).

Study design, population, and data collection Data from 14,689 subscribers to the biometric device platform WHOOP, Inc. (Boston, MA) were collected across a 1-year study (Sep 1, 2021 to Aug 31, 2022). During registration with WHOOP, participants reported their age and gender and provided written informed consent to allow the use of their deidentiﬁed data for research. Due to con- ﬁdentiality considerations, we did not have access to location data. Participant characteristics are presented in Table S1. Eligibility criteria required participants be ≥18 years of age, wear the biometric device for a minimum of 350 days (95.6% of total possible wear-time), and register ≥50 exercise activities within the analysis window of 10-h before to 2-h after habitual sleep onset to construct a sample of physically active individuals (i.e., with an exercise frequency of approximately one or more activities weekly) and to allow for within-person comparisons of different exercise timings and levels of exercise strain. Exercises outside this window were excluded. The ﬁnal dataset included 4,084,354 person-nights of data (Fig. 3 presents CONSORT ﬂow diagram). Table S12 includes demographic information for the included and excluded participants. A multi-sensor wrist-worn biometric device (WHOOP versions 3.0 or 4.0; Boston, MA) that captures continuous heart rate, accelerometer, and three-axis gyroscope data was used to derive exercise, cardiovascular, and sleep/wake metrics. This biometric device has been validated against electrocardiography and polysomnography for the assessment of heart rate (99% agreement) and 2-stage sleep categorisation (86–89% agreement), respectively24,36.

Exercise timing Exercise timing was operationalised using two reference points. In the primary analysis, exercise timing represented the conclusion of exercise relative to the participant’s habitual sleep onset. Individuals display a high degree of heterogeneity in sleep/wake timing37. What constitutes an evening exercise will depend on the typical sleep/wake patterns of the individual. Further, an individual’s sleep/wake timing can vary by season38 and by weekday/weekend37. Therefore, habitual sleep onset was quantiﬁed as the participant’s mean sleep onset of the corresponding calendar month and whether it was a weekday or weekend to account for seasonal variation and social jet lag. In the secondary analysis, exercise timing represented the conclusion of exercise relative to the participant’s sleep onset on that night. This method provides important context for how long it can take to recover from varying levels of exercise strain before sleep.

Exercise strain Exercise activities were logged manually on the WHOOP smartphone app or detected automatically by the WHOOP analytics platform and then conﬁrmed by the participant. Multiple exercise activities logged within 60-minutes of each other were treated as one activity. Activities less than 1-minute in duration and relaxation exercises, including yoga, stretching, meditation, and massage therapy were excluded from the analysis. Continuous heart rate data during each exercise activity were used to calculate durations spent in six heart rate zones (zones 0-5). Heart rate zones were determined as a percentage of the participant’s maximal heart rate (HRmax), where zone 0 = < 50% of HRmax, zone 1 = 50–60%, zone 2 = 60–70%, zone 3 = 70–80%, zone 4 = 80–90%, and zone 5 = 90–100%. HRmax was determined using the non-linear formula, 192–0.007 × age[239, or manually set by the participant, or automatically set to the maximal recorded heart rate. Exercise strain was quantiﬁed using summated-heart-rate-zones scores (SHRZS)40. # Noninvasive Impedance Analysis During S‐ICD Insertion Provides Justification for Defibrillation Based Testing Deferment

**Authors:** Andreas G Kontopidis; Mark É Czeisler; David H Yoo; Olivia Whittaker; Daniel C Pipilas; Theofanie Mela

**Affiliations:** 1 Boston Scientific, Marlborough, Massachusetts, USA | 2 Harvard T H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3 Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4 Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5 Tufts University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Following subcutaneous implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (S‐ICD) insertion, induction of ventricular fibrillation (VF) and defibrillation threshold testing (DFT) is the standard of practice to assess system performance. In contrast, DFT testing is not routinely performed after transvenous ICD (T‐ICD) insertion, supported by literature that emphasizes negative clinical repercussions and reliability of noninvasive predictors of successful defibrillation. There is a paucity of data for both the trajectory of noninvasive low voltage (LV) impedance measurements at S‐ICD insertion through the time of potential DFT testing and for the proximity of LV impedance measurements and high voltage (HV) shock impedance from 65J DFT or 10J testing.

We aim to characterize the trend in LV impedance from initial S‐ICD connection (LV T0) to final intraprocedural impedance (LV T4) and to compare LV impedance with HV impedance.

Data from patients who underwent S‐ICD implantation between July 2022 and March 2024 were analyzed. LV impedance measurements were collected during implant and HV impedance measurements were collected if 65J DFT/10J testing was performed. Differences in mean impedances at each time point were evaluated using paired t‐tests. For those who underwent 10J or 65J DFT testing, LV impedance was compared with HV impedance.

The primary analytic sample included 53 patients, with a mean age of 51 ± 15.7 years; 16 (30.2%) were female. LV impedance decreased by a mean of 14.5 ± 9.8 ohms (18.3%; p <0.001) from S‐ICD connection (T0) to the final intraprocedural measurement, approximately 60 min postimplant (T4). Among 35 patients who underwent HV testing (65J DFT or 10J), LV impedance at T4 and HV impedance did not differ significantly (1.7 ± 6.3 ohms; p = 0.116).

Our findings demonstrate a predictable reduction in LV impedance from S‐ICD connection to subsequent intraprocedural measurements. We also found that LV impedance at LV T4, the final intraprocedural measurement, did not significantly differ from contemporaneous HV impedance. Together, these findings indicate that LV impedance at implant can be expected to decline, and that 60‐min postimplant LV impedance may reliably approximate HV impedance. Evaluation of circumstances in which LV impedance could influence the decision to perform DFT testing is warranted.

## Introduction

Transvenous implantable cardioverter defibrillators (T‐ICDs) are fundamental in the clinical management of electrical cardiovascular pathologies, as they facilitate continuous intracardiac monitoring and terminate potentially rapid‐onset and life‐threatening cardiovascular arrhythmias. Clinical workflow during implantation of T‐ICDs has evolved through efforts to accurately and noninvasively determine device placement and device functionality after implantation [1]. In the early stages of T‐ICDs in the 1980s [2], nearly all patients who received T‐ICDs immediately underwent high voltage (HV) defibrillation threshold testing (DFT), plus 3‐ to 6‐week postimplantation testing through noninvasive programmed simulation DFTs (NIPS DFTs) [1]. These tests were performed to ensure that implanted devices could appropriately detect and respond to ventricular fibrillation in the event a patient went into a life‐threatening arrhythmia outside of a controlled clinical setting [3].

Over time, progression in T‐ICD system technology, including reversible biphasic waveform shock polarity, anatomical shocking vector placement congruence, and MADIT‐RIT standardized therapy zone programing drastically increased shock conversion reliability and efficacy [4, 5]. Subsequently, T‐ICD system placement became even more reliable and predictable with the addition of novel diagnostic capabilities emerging, including noninvasive low voltage (LV) impedance measurements to provide a pseudo shock impedance metric without requiring DFTs and a HV shock. Alternatives to HV DFTs are particularly desirable given the short and long‐term negative clinical repercussions associated with DFT testing, as well as increased healthcare resource utilization and costs [1]. Encouragingly, a study of 332 patients found that the success of shocks for clinically significant arrhythmias was the same for patients who underwent full DFT (91%; n = 129) and for those who did not have any form of DFT (92%; n = 203) [1], providing evidence to support deferment of DFT testing immediately following T‐ICD implantation [6]. In response to a growing evidence base, clinical practice following T‐ICD implantation has largely shifted to deferment of DFTs and NIPS testing [3], with the exception of right sided implants, subcutaneous defibrillators, and patients at higher risk [7]. DFT testing is based on probabilistic values, but DFT testing is no longer routinely recommended in patients undergoing left‐sided T‐ICD implantation. This has in turn decreased the clinical application of HV impedance as a surrogate for successful DFT testing in T‐ICDs, however, the association of HV impedance during Emblem Subcutaneous ICD (S‐ICD) insertions is still under investigation [3].

In comparison to postimplantation DFT testing for T‐ICDs, less evidence exists for DFT testing with S‐ICD, for which clinical practice includes DFT testing post‐implant in the vast majority of cases [3], and is still the device manufacturer recommendation [8]. Attempts to utilize acute lower energy shocks to determine HV impedance and DFT conversion probability have been made, including a study that shows no statistical difference in conversion probability between less energy shocks (10J) to full energy shocks (80J) at the time of implant [9]. Continuing this precedent, the need for further investigation regarding the use of noninvasive LV metrics as an HV impedance surrogate is of clinical importance for S‐ICD implant technique progression, and DFT testing deferment. Lack of this evidence is partly due to the novelty of the system and to its unique implant technique, which avoids all transvenous access sites to provide defibrillation therapy via entirely extra‐thoracic placement. To achieve this goal, the S‐ICD provides a larger therapy output of 80J vs the transvenous 41J standard, requiring an increased size of the device. Since its adoption, implant techniques, studies, and technological advancements have led to significant evolution of the S‐ICD system [10]. Previously recommended 3‐incision techniques with the defibrillating coil placed left lateral of the sternum and subcutaneous pocket formation have now transitioned to an intermuscular pocket formation between the serratus and latissimus dorsi, and a 2‐incision technique with heightened focused on reducing depth of adipose tissue between the coil and sternum in a more medial position to mitigate propagation of myopotentials in the context of an indexed PRAETORIAN score [11]. These procedural improvements have led to lower impedance values, lower inappropriate shock rates, and more optimal sensing, with comparable clinical results to T‐ICDs demonstrated through the PRAETORIAN and ATLAS trials [12].

Much like improvements throughout the longevity of T‐ICD system placements, improvements of the S‐ICD system have led to increased confidence and predictability in anatomical vector positioning of the S‐ICD system, leading to higher shock conversion efficacy [13]. Device algorithms and diagnostic features have also progressed; the SMART pass filter algorithm introduced in 2016, which was followed with the UNTOUCHED and EFFORTLESS clinical trials, found noninferiority in inappropriate shock rates and lead related complication rates compared to T‐ICDs [12].

Most recently, in 2022, the MILAN update provided a novel noninvasive diagnostic capability of LV impedance measurements, like that of T‐ICDs. In the wake of these advancements in predictability of conversion success due to procedural improvements, algorithm enhancements, and clinical trials; exploration of the potential for minimizing DFT testing for the S‐ICD system is warranted. To date, the evidence base consists primarily of the EMILY abstract, which reported findings from 41 patients who underwent S‐ICD implantation with MILAN LV impedance measurements. The investigators found that LV impedances were within 10 ohms of HV shock impedances in 83% of patients, with a strong correlation overall (Pearson r = 0.889) [14]. Given that patients with below 90‐ohm HV impedance have a greater than 90% probability of S‐ICD DFT conversion success [14, 15], and that univariate analysis has demonstrated that HV impedance values above 138 ohms predict high DFT test values and low conversion probability [16], accurate LV impedance measurements with meaningful correlation to the HV impedance has prognostic value [17]. Further assessment of MILAN LV impedance measurements in larger clinical samples with more comprehensive characterization of measurements, including temporal trends, is necessary to provide insights into the accuracy of the LV impedance measurements and how they may be used in clinical practice. We therefore sought to characterize the trend in LV impedance from initial connection of device (LV T0) to final intraprocedural impedance (LV T4), and to further correlate LV impedance with HV shock impedance.

## Methods

This was a retrospective observational study within Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB) care centers in the United States. Eligible participants included patients who had received a newly implanted S‐ICD following the implementation of the March 2022 MILAN upgrade, after which time LV impedance measurements were made available through the device. All consecutive patients that underwent S‐ICD insertion between July 2022 and March 2024 at Massachusetts General Hospital were included in this study, with no exclusion upon later review. Impedance measurements were documented day of S‐ICD insertion to avoid potential residual confounding from retrospective analysis.

All study data, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), S‐ICD implantation date, intermuscular or subcutaneous pocket formation, intraoperative LV impedance measurements (timepoints relative to device implantation: T0 [0 m], T1 [5 m], T2 [10 m], T3 [30 m], T4 [60 m]), 10J HV impedance, and 65J DFT HV impedance were extracted from the electronic medical record using Massachusetts General Hospital's D4Q clinical data warehouse. LV impedance measurements are generated by the S‐ICD system through administration of a sub‐threshold 4 V output at 2 µs to generate a pseudo shock impedance value of proximity to that generated from a HV (10J or 65J DFT) therapy. A variable of HV impedance was created with 65J DFT testing, or with a 10J shock if conducted, since there is evidence of no statistically significant differences in the average impedance values between the two [9].

Data from patients who met the inclusion criteria during the study were included and comprised the primary analytic sample. Two additional subsamples were created: (1) patients who underwent HV testing (HV subsample) and (2) patients who had measures at all timepoints and underwent DFT testing. Because collection of these measurements was not mutually exclusive, data from patients could be present in all three samples.

For the primary analysis, descriptive statistics were used to characterize the absolute and relative trends of intraprocedural LV impedance measurements (T0 through T4), including mean ± SD among all patients as well as absolute and relative delta impedance, defined as change in within‐participant measurements of post‐implant impedance at T0 and each of T1 through T4. For each comparison, paired t‐tests were used to identify statistically significant difference in delta impedance. Linear regression modeling was used to assess for a statistically significant relationship between LV impedance measurements at T0 as the explanatory variable and at T4, the last intraprocedural measure, as the dependent variable. Models were constructed as univariate for the primary analysis and multivariate, with age, sex, BMI, and pocket formation as covariates.

Within the HV subsample, descriptive statistics were used to compare high voltage testing impedance measures with T0 and T4, respectively. Paired t‐tests were used to compare delta impedances, and univariate and multivariate regression models were used with HV impedance measures as dependent variables and T0 and T4 as independent variables in separate models. The percentage of intraprocedural impedance measures within 5 or 10 ohms of HV testing measures was also calculated. For exploratory analyses, intraprocedural LV impedance measurements were compared by age (categorized), sex, BMI, and pocket formation in the primary analytic sample.

As these data were generated through standard clinical operations, specific informed consent for this study protocol was not required. The protocol was reviewed by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Boards and met criteria for exemption (45 CFR 46) as a secondary research protocol. Analyses were conducted using Python software (version 3.8.8; Python Software Foundation) using the statsmodels module (version 0.12.2). A p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
