## Discussion

In this retrospective study of 53 S‐ICD recipients, we found that LV impedance measurements decreased by nearly 20% on average in the hour following S‐ICD implantation, and that this decline leads to convergence of LV and HV impedance measurements one‐hour post‐implantation. As a result, whereas only one‐quarter of LV measurements obtained immediately post‐implant were within 10 ohms of HV measurements, nearly 90% of LV measurements obtained one‐hour post‐implant from the same patients were within this range. Together, these findings reveal a characterizable temporal trend of LV impedance measurements and indicate that LV measurements may approximate HV measurements after a decline post‐implantation. While the technical and patient factors underlying this decline require further investigation, the predictability of S‐ICD intraprocedural LV impedance trends and its association with HV impedance is of clinical importance, as its exploration as a reliable metric could impact decision‐making on DFT deferment following S‐ICD implantation.

Technical factors related to the S‐ICD implantation process could influence the trajectory of LV impedance values. For example, air entrapment and inappropriate electrode contact with adipose tissue may diminish the accuracy of LV system impedance measurements [18]. Air entrapment was an early cause of inappropriate S‐ICD function due to intermittent and transient effects of the entrapped air on the sensing process. It is plausible that the prevalence of undetected acute and transient air entrapment in the subcutaneous space is high, with large‐volume physiologic absorption and resolution of residual air immediately post‐implantation with continued gradual reabsorption at a lower rate thereafter, as evidenced by 99% resolution of entrapped air within one week of the procedure based on computed tomography imaging [19]. The considerable decline in entrapped air in the immediate post‐implant phase could partially account for the high‐magnitude reduction in LV measures.

Pocket formation and tunneling from the xiphoid incision to the pocket, as well as superiorly up the sternum, introduces the potential for multiple air tracts in adipose tissue, limiting optimal electrode contact with the tissue, reducing LV impedance accuracy. Specifically, effective defibrillation is based on delivery of an electrical shock to a critical amount of myocardial cells, which is determined by the flow of electrical current and resistance on the circuit [20]. The impact optimal electrode contact can have on defibrillation success can be appreciated when considering conventional, hand‐held defibrillator paddles, where increases in pressure force increases electrode‐skin contact levels while decreasing air volume in the lungs, thus, requiring different paddle forces for adults as compared with children [20]. One possible approach to further accelerate this air dispersion could be the administration of saline within the sheath of the delivery system, prior to introducing the electrode. Following the insertion of the electrode, massaging the sternum to disperse residual air entrapment created during tunneling and utilizing saline's conductive properties could accelerate the LV impedance trajectory by providing better electrode contact. Further investigation is required to analyze the effect air dispersion and fluid dynamics have on the rate and absolute value of intraprocedural LV system impedance measurements during S‐ICD implantation.

Our exploratory findings comparing subcutaneous versus intermuscular device placement suggest that while the rate of regression of impedance from initial connection of the device to final closure did not change between pocket formation groups, the intermuscular pocket formation group, which is found deeper in the body tucked between muscle groups, could be associated with overall lower LV impedance values. In one study with more than 1500 patients, patients with intermuscular pocket formation showed lower inappropriate shock rates compared to that of subcutaneous pocket formation, indicating precedent for pocket formations influencing system performance [21]. More research is required to determine statistical significance of LV impedance values and trends for differing pocket formations, specifically, within the scope of temporal air entrapment dissipation as well as device‐skin electrode contact. Aside from air entrapment and pocket formation; device temperature, as the device equilibrates from its storage to body temperature, could play a role in optimizing electrode contact and accuracy of intraprocedural LV impedance trends and values [18]. Dense fibrous encapsulation has been reported post S‐ICD system implantation, leading to high HV impedance values and failed DFT testing [16]. Additional studies report long‐term impedance rise post S‐ICD implant, along with the impact revascularized device pouches may have on mitigating capsule formation and reducing impedance values [22]. Our study did not investigate long‐term outcomes, and further studies are needed to determine whether acute DFT testing has any correlation with capsule formation and long‐term impedance trends.

Patient factors such as BMI, sex, and age could also be influential in the decline and absolute values of intraprocedural S‐ICD impedances from the time of device connection to final closure. A positive correlation between high BMI and high DFT has been demonstrated in previous studies [23]. The elevated DFT in obese patients could be related to the presence of increased adipose tissue, which is a poor electrical conductor. Studies have shown that during an 80J cardioversion administered by the S‐ICD system, varying electrical conductivity within different tissue densities, such as adipose tissue, will inherently have higher resistance to electrical conductivity, compared to less dense parts of the body such as bone [23, 24]. Our exploratory analysis findings were concurrent with this precedent; however, larger patient populations are required to have sufficiently powered testing for statistically significant differences.

Patients with BMI classification of obese had statistically significant higher T0 and T4 values, as well as a larger overage decrease from T0 to T4, compared to BMI's classified as healthy or overweight. During S‐ICD electrode implantation, any increased amount of adipose between the sternum and electrode has shown to increase system impedance [24]. More investigation is required, specifically, targeting the impact increased adipose tissue directly above the sternum has on intraprocedural LV impedance values and its trends. These exploratory findings indicate that the excess adipose tissue in obese BMI patients could be associated with overall higher intraprocedural LV impedance measurements.

Aside from BMI, patient factors such as sex and age could play an influence on the intraprocedural and long‐term LV impedance measurements. Previous studies have indicated that female LV impedances were significantly associated with increased impedance over >2 year periods post procedurally [22]. In our exploratory findings, males reported higher mean T0 and T4 LV impedance values compared to females, however, larger patient populations are required for statistical significance. Aside from operator technique to ensure optimal S‐ICD system placement, patient factors such as BMI, sex, age, and perhaps scar tissue and septal/posterior wall thickness, require further analysis to determine their impact on intraprocedural LV impedance trends and absolute values.

Beyond patient and technical factors that influence intraprocedural LV and HV impedance values, S‐ICD system DFT conversion probability is also influenced by anatomical system placement. Relative to the T‐ICD system, the S‐ICD system lacks the breadth of randomized controlled trials and studies that identify potential markers of DFT conversion success. For example, there is a significant impact of anatomical lead placement, specifically aligning the shocking vector with the apex of the heart when evaluating conversion probability [13]. The T‐ICD shocking vector must transverse directly through myocardial tissue within the heart, which is historically susceptible to variance among LV mass between ischemic and nonischemic hearts [25]. Conversely, the S‐ICD system avoids the vasculature and heart entirely and sits subcutaneously above the sternum in adipose tissue. Encouragingly, PRAETORIAN scores have been validated for the implantation of the S‐ICD system, in which LV mass does not appear to be a factor for successful DFTs [11]. The difference of surrounding myocardial (T‐ICDs) versus adipose (S‐ICDs) tissue, and respective shocking vector relationship, could influence conversion probability success, even with adequate HV and LV impedance values. More studies, specifically with the S‐ICD system, are required to determine if these associated factors outside of impedance values influence conversion probability.

Strengths of this study include the novel findings of a characterizable regression in impedance from connection of the device to final intraprocedural measurements, as well as an augmented correlation between LV and HV impedance measurements previously investigated. These findings further strengthen the utility of LV impedance measurements at the time of S‐ICD system insertion as a modality to accurately assess system integrity and influence DFT testing deferment in clinical practice in the scope of patient safety and procedural efficiency.

Limitations of the study include the lack of a demographically representative sample as well as a small cell count, specifically, for the HV impedance analytic group (N = 35) and within exploratory subgroup analysis (BMI, sex, age, and pocket formation) for statistical significance. Similarly, a larger patient population would aid in strengthening the findings of regression of LV impedances within the primary analytic group (N = 53), although the patient population in this group did meet our power analysis requirements. LV impedances collected by the S‐ICD system have lower resolution (range of 5 ohms per data collection) compared to that of HV impedances (range of 1 ohm per data point), decreasing confidence intervals of LV to HV comparisons. Retrospective studies are observational and subject to bias due to unmeasured confounding, so the findings in this manuscript are correlational rather than causal. Future studies designed for causal analysis could test the hypotheses generated from this study. Additionally, time intervals utilized in this study (T0–T4) were developed to normalize for operator and implant time. The closing process for the SICD generator has variability between implanters. Factors associated with this variability include the decision to tie down the device to the pocket, the number of layers to close, and if/when DFT testing is performed. The variability of these factors will have an influence on the time to final closure of the pocket and the normalization of the time intervals utilized in this study (T0–T4).

In conclusion, the results of our primary analytic sample (N = 53) demonstrate a predictable regression in LV impedance (14.5 ± 9.8 ohms, p < 0.001; −18.3%, p < 0.001) from first connection of device, T0, to subsequent final intraprocedural measurements, T4. High voltage subgroup analysis (N = 35) found a statistically significant correlation between LV T4, the final intraprocedural low voltage impedance, and HV shock impedances impedance (−1.7 ± 6.3 ohms; p = 0.116; −2.2%, p = 0.19). This study showed a characterizable regression of intraoperative LV impedances, while further correlating LV impedances with HV impedance. This strengthened correlation, in unison with existing HV impedance precedent, allows for the opportunity for noninvasive LV impedances to be considered in the decision making of procedural DFT testing. Initiatives for utilizing lower energy 10J shocks as a replacement for DFT testing have already taken form [9]; however, official recommendations by the device manufacturer are still to perform DFT tests post implantation of S‐ICD system insertion [8]. More studies are required to further strengthen the clinical trajectory of utilizing lower energy or potentially noninvasive LV impedance metrics as a modality to justify the deferment of DFT testing. DFT testing has been shown to have negative long‐term patient safety repercussions, increase in acute procedural risks, as well as an increase burden on hospital resources, time, and procedural efficiency [1].
